name: Telegraph cryptic crossword, All New book 4 No 26

book.title: The Telegraph All New Cryptic Crosswords 4

clue.text: Spend all one's money and let everyone go hang

blocks.note: first meaning: blow is slang for squander, so this is to squander everything
second meaning: blow as a mild oath, as in 'blow them all', dismissing the whole lot

explanation.surface: A reckless spender empties the bank account and stops caring what anyone thinks.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase works twice: 'blow' means squander, and 'blow ...!' is also a dismissive British oath, so 'blow the lot' can mean 'damn the lot of them'.
explanation.definitionFit: To blow money is slang for squandering it, so blowing the whole lot means spending every penny at once.

blocks.note: first meaning: Alexander Graham, credited with inventing the telephone
second meaning: a phone call, as in 'give me a ring'

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one person's ringtone; the two halves are a surname and a slang word for a phone call.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of the telephone pioneer is also British slang for a phone call, as in 'give me a bell'.

clue.text: Said periods of time belonging to us

indicators.note: said means spoken, so the word is identified by how it is pronounced rather than spelt

blocks.note: periods of sixty minutes; the h of this word is silent

explanation.surface: A family claims its spare time as its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Ours is the possessive pronoun for the first person plural, meaning owned by us.

indicators.note: something mislaid is put in the wrong place, so these letters end up out of their original positions

blocks.note: the six letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A mother or father has lost a piece of a surgeon's kit.
explanation.definitionFit: A trepan is a cylindrical saw surgeons once used to bore holes in the skull, so it is a medical instrument.

blocks.note: the surface reading: a cry of total bafflement
the setter's reading: the clue really is nothing but a punctuation symbol, so the answer names that symbol

explanation.walkthrough: The setter pretends to have no clue to offer, and the one thing printed after the words is the thing to name: the punctuation sign itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The symbol printed at the end of the clue is the punctuation sign used after exclamations, which is exactly what the answer names.

clue.text: Able to become a monastic devotee

indicators.note: to become something is to turn into it, so these letters are turned into a different word

blocks.note: both words are the fodder

explanation.surface: A person qualified to enter a religious order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Able to' reads as a phrase needing a verb; both words are just letters, and 'become' is the shuffle signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An oblate is a layperson dedicated to the religious life, attached to a monastery without taking full vows.

blocks.note: first sense: the French word for 'we'
second sense: an English word, borrowed from Greek, for common sense or gumption

explanation.surface: A boast that the French are a clever people.
explanation.walkthrough: The same four letters are the French pronoun and an informal English noun, so the clue runs a foreign word into an English one.
explanation.definitionFit: Nous is informal British English for practical good sense or shrewdness, from the Greek word for mind.

blocks.note: on top of, as in 'over' the table
a duty is a levy or fee, which is a charge

explanation.surface: A crooked employee rips off customers during working hours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On duty' looks like a single phrase meaning at work; it splits into two separate words, and a duty here is a tax on goods.
explanation.definitionFit: To overcharge is to demand too high a price, which is a way of cheating customers.

clue.text: Yet fans set out to take precautionary measures

indicators.note: set out here suggests laid out afresh, so the letters are arranged in a new order

blocks.note: all ten letters of these three words

explanation.surface: Supporters nonetheless go out of their way to guard against trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set out' reads as a phrasal verb, but 'set' is the last word of the fodder and 'out' alone is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally nets that catch falling acrobats, safety nets figuratively are safeguards put in place in case things go wrong.

definitions.note: adjective describing maps; the answer qualifies them

blocks.note: first meaning: the term for maps drawn at a high ratio, showing a small area in fine detail
second meaning: in everyday use, wide-ranging or done in a big way

explanation.surface: A comment that certain maps cover a lot of ground.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that a map of this kind actually shows a small area, enlarged; the adjective in general use means the opposite, broad in scope.
explanation.definitionFit: In ordinary use the compound adjective describes something done in a big way, which is what extensive means.

blocks.note: first meaning: food, here meat from cattle
second meaning: slang for a grievance or grumble

explanation.surface: A restaurant dish that has diners grumbling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fare' looks like a ticket price, but it means food; the second word is slang for a grudge, as in 'what's your problem?'.
explanation.definitionFit: The meat of cattle is a kind of fare, and the same word is informal for a grievance someone nurses.

clue.text: Film award given to utterly unrestrained author

indicators.note: utterly hints at uttering, speaking out, so the next word counts by its sound

blocks.note: the Academy Award statuette is called an Oscar
wild means unrestrained, and the surname is pronounced the same

explanation.surface: An Academy Award goes to a completely uninhibited writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Utterly' looks like an intensifier for 'unrestrained', but it signals speech: utter means to say aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: Oscar Wilde was the Irish playwright and novelist of The Importance of Being Earnest, so he is an author.

clue.text: Haggard rogue has to swear nothing to us

blocks.note: a cad is a dishonourable man
to aver is to declare solemnly
zero, shaped like the letter O
taken as written

explanation.surface: A worn-out villain must take an oath that he owes the speakers nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Haggard' might suggest H. Rider Haggard the novelist, but it is simply the adjective meaning gaunt.
explanation.definitionFit: Cadaverous means corpse-like, pale and gaunt, so it describes someone who looks haggard.

clue.text: Game played in a street in Galilean town

indicators.note: a game played in a place happens inside it, so the middle pieces sit within the town

blocks.note: the town in Galilee where, in the Gospel, water was turned into wine
taken as written
standard abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: Children playing some game in the street of a biblical town.
explanation.walkthrough: Cana is the Galilee town of the wedding where water became wine in John's Gospel; the town's letters split to hold the street.
explanation.definitionFit: Canasta is a rummy-style card game played with two packs, so it is a specific example of a game.

blocks.note: first meaning: to link two things together physically
second meaning: to relate one idea to another in the mind

explanation.walkthrough: Both words are verbs here: 'associate' could be read as a noun meaning a colleague, but it is the mental act of linking.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both fastening things together and mentally linking one idea with another.

definitions.note: a noun phrase for a perfect being; the answer is the matching compound

blocks.note: first meaning: wholly good, without any flaw
second meaning: a name for the herb Good-King-Henry, a kind of goosefoot

explanation.walkthrough: The plant name is obscure: it is an old country name for Good-King-Henry, a leafy goosefoot once eaten like spinach.
explanation.definitionFit: Something entirely good has no flaw, which is what perfect means; the same compound is also a folk name for a herb.

blocks.note: first meaning: a period of the year, such as the holiday or football calendar
second meaning: to flavour food

explanation.surface: A cook announcing the moment to spice up the dish.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a noun for a recurring period of time and a verb for flavouring food with salt, pepper or spices.

blocks.note: E is the international vehicle code for Spain (España)
licit means lawful or allowed

explanation.surface: Spanish authorities give approval for gathering intelligence.
explanation.definitionFit: To elicit is to draw out a response or facts from someone, which is obtaining information.

clue.text: Has treating Gina badly been out of character?

indicators.note: something done badly is botched, so the letters before it come out in a mangled order

blocks.note: all fifteen letters of these three words are the fodder

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether mistreating Gina was unlike the usual behaviour of the person concerned.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers the slightly loose definition: something that goes against the grain is contrary to one's nature.
explanation.definitionFit: An action that runs contrary to a person's natural inclinations is said to go against their grain, i.e. out of keeping with their nature.

blocks.note: W is the standard abbreviation for wife
to retch is to heave as if being sick

explanation.surface: A villain so loathsome that his wife is physically sickened.
explanation.definitionFit: A wretch is a contemptible or despicable person, a synonym for a rogue or villain.

clue.text: Intuitive feeling about a cut of meat

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece is wrapped round the other

blocks.note: a gut feeling or suspicion
taken as written; it does double duty as the definition's article

explanation.surface: A cook has a gut feeling about which joint to buy.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' is borrowed from the definition and slipped inside: H(A)UNCH.
explanation.definitionFit: A haunch is the leg and loin of an animal, especially venison, served as a joint of meat.

indicators.note: the head of a word is its front, so only the opening letter of skin is used

blocks.note: the word skin, of which only the head is kept
ought expresses obligation, just as should does

explanation.surface: A warning that a shaven-headed thug ought to be chased down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skinhead' reads as one word, but it splits into a source word and a front-letter instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Sought is the past participle of seek, and something sought after has been searched for or chased.

clue.text: Godly attendant uses strange turn of phrase

indicators.note: a strange turn gives the letters an odd twist, putting them in a new order

blocks.note: the six letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A heavenly servant speaks in an odd idiom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn of phrase' is a fixed expression meaning a way of speaking; split, 'strange turn of' is the signal and 'phrase' is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Seraphs are the highest order of angels, attending on the throne of God in Isaiah's vision.

clue.text: Teased relative in short man's embrace

indicators.note: an embrace wraps arms around someone, so one piece is held inside the other

blocks.note: Ted is a short form of Edward or Theodore, a shortened man's name
an aunt is a family relative

explanation.surface: Someone mocked for being hugged by a small man who is a relation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short man' does not mean a small person: it is a pet name cut down from a longer one, here Edward.
explanation.definitionFit: To taunt is to jeer or provoke with insults, so taunted is a stronger synonym for teased.

blocks.note: first meaning: the North American name for the diver, a fish-eating water bird
second meaning: informal for a crazy or foolish person, as in 'loony'

explanation.surface: A scornful remark about an American deep-sea diver's intelligence.
explanation.walkthrough: The diver is a bird, not a person: the bird the British call a diver is called a loon in North America.
explanation.definitionFit: Loon is a dated informal word for a silly or crazy person, so it fits as a synonym for idiot.

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a tin or can is a container

explanation.surface: A little box in a room for reading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Study' looks like a room, as in a den, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To scan a document is to examine it closely, so it means study.

blocks.note: O is a standard abbreviation for old
DD is a Doctor of Divinity, so DDs are theologians

explanation.surface: Elderly theologians gambling.
explanation.walkthrough: DD stands for Doctor of Divinity, a senior degree in theology.
explanation.definitionFit: The odds are the likelihood of something happening, which is what chances means.

clue.text: An Italian graduate cut for being deranged

blocks.note: un is the Italian for 'a' or 'an'
a BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a graduate
lanced means pierced or cut with a blade, as a boil is

explanation.surface: An Italian student is sacked from a course because of a mental breakdown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'An Italian' is not a person here; it asks for the Italian word for 'an'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone mentally unbalanced is unstable in mind, which is what deranged describes.

indicators.note: part-time suggests only a portion, so just part of the words that follow is taken

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of models and the start of earn

explanation.surface: Models who work only some of the time are paid better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Earn more' reads as a pair, but the last word is the definition, and the letters sit across the gap between the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Else means other or additional, as in 'anything else?', so it stands in for more.

blocks.note: to shake someone is to shock or unsettle them
hands are manual workers, as in farm hands

explanation.surface: A boss makes peace after a dispute, then rattles the staff.
explanation.definitionFit: Clasping hands is the traditional gesture of making peace or sealing an agreement after a quarrel.
